name: memento
intent: Capture an object's internal state in an opaque, self-contained snapshot that only the object itself can interpret, so the state can be restored later without exposing - or letting the history keeper tamper with - the object's private data.
problem: A feature must be able to put an object back into an earlier state: the user undoes an edit, a multi-step operation rolls back after a failed step, a form edit is cancelled, or a simulation returns to a checkpoint. Copying the state from the outside means publishing private data and coupling every client to the state's shape; handing out a live reference to the state lets whoever stores the history mutate it; and a shallow copy keeps aliasing the state it was supposed to freeze, so 'undo' silently restores the present instead of the past.
context: Applies where the object owning the state can both produce and consume a snapshot, but the component that decides when to save or restore it - an undo stack, a command, a transaction coordinator, a wizard - must not read or rewrite the captured data. Works for in-memory history (bounded stacks, checkpoints) and for persisted history (serialized snapshots for autosave or session restore); it captures one originator at a time, not a distributed transaction.
benefits: Encapsulation is preserved: the originator decides what a snapshot contains, so private fields never become part of a public state API, and only the originator can interpret a memento.

History management is decoupled from state shape: the caretaker stores, orders, labels and discards opaque mementos, so stacks, redo, grouping and depth limits can be built and changed independently of the originator's fields.
Adding or removing state touches the originator and its memento only; code that merely keeps history stays untouched, and the copy logic lives where the invariants are known.

Undo composes with commands: a command can hold the memento it needs to reverse itself, which makes transaction-like grouping, macros and redo feasible without each command re-implementing state capture.
Restoring re-establishes derived and protected invariants in one place, because the originator applies the snapshot itself instead of a generic field copy from outside.
tradeoffs: Snapshots duplicate state: memory and copy time grow with history depth times state size, and saving on every change can dominate an application's footprint; deltas, structural sharing or invertible commands are the escape hatches, each adding complexity.
The caretaker owns the memento lifecycle: unbounded stacks, or snapshots of originators that no longer exist, leak memory and can resurrect stale data that should have been discarded.

A whole-object snapshot is conservative and only rolls back what it captured; side effects already performed outside the captured state (messages sent, files written, resources acquired) are not undone, so partial rollback can leave the system inconsistent.
The encapsulation guarantee is only as strong as the language: dynamic languages cannot stop a caretaker from poking at a memento, and shallow copies leak the live state even in static ones.

Two extra roles and a save/restore discipline must be maintained in parallel with the state, and a memento applied to the wrong originator instance or created before an invariant was re-established silently corrupts history.

participants.responsibility: Owns the state: creates a memento capturing exactly the data that constitutes that state, and restores itself from a memento it previously produced, re-establishing its invariants in one place.

Immutable value carrying the snapshot; exposes its contents through a wide interface only to the originator and a narrow interface (metadata such as label or timestamp) to everyone else, and is never modified after construction.

Decides when a memento is taken and when one is restored, and stores mementos (bounded stack, command, transaction, history file); it may hold, label, order and discard them but never inspects or alters their contents.
Triggers the operation that changes the originator and asks the caretaker to save, undo or redo; it never reads or writes mementos directly.

use_cases: Undo/redo in editors (text, drawing, CAD, spreadsheets, IDEs): the document or selection is the originator; the undo manager or the command that performed the edit is the caretaker. VS Code, IntelliJ, Vim, and Emacs all implement variants of this.
Transactional rollback: snapshot an aggregate root before a multi-step operation and restore it when a later step fails, replacing per-step compensating-code with a single restore.
Simulation and game checkpoints, including deterministic replay: snapshot world state at intervals and use a seed value as the memento that reproduces an exact sequence of pseudo-random numbers.
Wizards, settings dialogs and property panels: snapshot the pristine state on open and restore it on cancel, so no component has to reach into the model or know which fields to reset.
Autosave and session restore: persist serialized mementos so the last N editing steps survive a restart, with the history replayed through the originator on session resume.
Tooling around a domain object (preview, dry-run, migration): capture state, run the experiment, then roll back on demand rather than rebuilding the object from scratch.
Database transaction savepoints: each SAVEPOINT name maps to a memento of the connection's or transaction's state, and ROLLBACK TO restores without discarding the whole transaction.

Feature-flag or A/B-test evaluation context: snapshot the evaluation environment before applying a variant and restore it afterward, so flags evaluated inside a test do not leak into production state.
Networked game state reconciliation: snapshot client-side entity state before server corrections arrive; if the correction is rejected (optimistic concurrency), restore from the local memento.
Form/state validation preview: snapshot the live form state before applying a validation transform; if validation fails, restore the original state rather than re-rendering from scratch.

ML hyperparameter tuning and experiment tracking: snapshot model weights, training configuration, and dataset version as a memento; restore to compare against subsequent experiments or to recover from a crashed training run.

Configuration management and infrastructure-as-code dry runs: snapshot the current cluster or service configuration, apply proposed changes, validate outcomes, and restore from the snapshot if the change is rejected or causes drift.

Document collaboration conflict resolution: snapshot a user's local edits before applying a server-side merge; if the merge produces conflicts, restore the local snapshot and prompt the user rather than silently discarding changes.

Financial transaction rollback in trading systems: snapshot account state or order book depth before submitting a batch of orders; if risk limits are breached mid-batch, roll back to the snapshot and cancel pending orders.

UI state preservation across orientation changes or theme switches on mobile: snapshot widget tree state, apply orientation or theme change, restore from snapshot if the change corrupts layout or causes crashes.

Unity Editor object editing: Unity's official Undo.RecordObject API captures an object's pre-edit state for the editor undo stack; the caretaker-like editor history restores the object without callers copying its private fields.

Apple Foundation/AppKit undo management: UndoManager groups registered reversible changes into undo and redo stacks, giving a framework-level caretaker for grouped edits while targets own the state-changing operation.

PostgreSQL transaction checkpoints: SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT retain a named transaction position and restore commands after it; this is a database-scoped memento analogue, not a rollback for external side effects.
avoid_when: The object is immutable or its state is trivially recomputable: take a fresh value or recompute instead of keeping history.
A single reusable copy is needed, not a history: Prototype-style cloning (or a copy constructor) is the simpler alternative.
The changes are local to a few fields of a large state: record deltas or invertible commands rather than whole-state snapshots.

The captured object shares mutable state with other objects or holds live resources (open files, sockets, locks), so restoring it cannot restore the system; use a transaction or compensating actions instead.
The history must be inspected, queried or audited: the narrow interface is a liability, and an append-only event log or change records are the right artifact.
The requirement is only 'cancel before commit', which validation plus not committing achieves without any snapshot machinery.
anti_patterns: Exposing the memento's fields publicly (or for tests only): the caretaker and any client can then forge or tamper with history, and the pattern's encapsulation guarantee is gone.
Caretakers that keep every memento forever: unbounded growth, stale data resurrected by undo, and originators kept alive long after they were discarded.

Mementos that hold live references instead of a snapshot - MemberwiseClone shallow copies in C#, dup or a Struct of mutable members in Ruby, a list shared between Kotlin copy() results, an uncloned Go slice - so restoring yields the current state.
Snapshotting state that cannot be rolled back (files written, messages published, resources held) and presenting undo as if the system returned to the earlier state.
Duplicating the state into a parallel 'backup' object that is then mutated alongside the original, so the snapshot is no longer frozen.

Capturing open resources (file handles, sockets, database connections) in the memento: restoration re-establishes a handle that may be stale, broken, or point to a resource that was closed since the snapshot was taken.
Serializing mementos to disk without schema validation or version checks: a class evolution that changes the state shape renders older snapshots unreadable or silently corrupts restored state.
Capturing secrets, credentials, or tokens in the snapshot: persisted mementos become a security surface, and anyone with read access to the snapshot store can extract sensitive data.

Using memento for distributed transaction consistency: memento captures one object's state and cannot atomically roll back cross-service side effects (messages sent, downstream calls completed); partial rollback leaves the system in an inconsistent state.
Snapshotting the entire object graph when only a small portion changed: excessive memory use and copy latency in hot paths that call snapshot() on every operation.

Applying a memento from a different originator instance or an older class version: silent mismatches where restored state is misinterpreted because the memento's schema does not match the target object's expectations.
design_principles: Encapsulation and information hiding: the snapshot is produced and consumed by the owner of the state; everybody else sees an opaque value.
Single responsibility: the originator owns state and invariants, the caretaker owns history policy (when, how deep, how long).
High cohesion: the knowledge of which fields constitute the state lives with the state itself, where it stays correct as the state evolves.
Open/closed: new state fields change the originator and its memento, not the history machinery that stores them.
Value semantics: a memento is copied data, not a shared reference - immutability is what makes it a snapshot.
best_practices: Make the memento immutable: pass all captured data through the constructor and provide no setters; seal or freeze the type where the language supports it. Immutability is the foundation — a snapshot that mutates is not a snapshot.

Keep the memento type private to the originator (nested class, private constructor, unexported struct, closures in FP languages) or expose it through a marker interface that carries only metadata (label, timestamp, version), never internal state. The caretaker must never be able to forge or tamper with history.

Snapshot deeply and explicitly: copy collections, owned objects, and references — a shallow copy aliases mutable state, making undo silently restore the present instead of the past. For mutable collections inside mementos, prefer immutable collection types (ImmutableList in C#, tuple/frozen dataclass in Python, copy.of in Java) to avoid shared-state aliasing between live and saved states.

Bound the history (maximum depth, age, or memory budget) and release mementos when their originator is discarded; validate on restore that the memento belongs to this originator instance. Implement explicit retention policies: max count, max bytes, max age, or user-cleared. Unbounded stacks leak memory and resurrect stale data.
Let the originator create and apply mementos itself so that invariants and derived fields are re-established in one place; field-copying from the caretaker silently leaves derived state stale.

Measure before snapshotting hot paths: if copy time dominates, store deltas, share immutable structure (persistent data structures), or record invertible commands behind the same save/restore interface. Profile before adding delta or compression complexity — simple full snapshots are correct first.

Treat persisted mementos as untrusted input: avoid capturing secrets (passwords, tokens, keys) in snapshots unless restoration genuinely requires them; validate on restore and use schema checks or filters when deserializing from disk. Serialized mementos from untrusted sources can carry security risks.

Record snapshots at meaningful boundaries (not after every keystroke): batch micro-changes or record only after atomic operations complete, to keep history meaningful and bounded. Use debouncing — ignore captures that are too recent or originate from the same source — to prevent snapshot storms.

For complex object graphs, consider incremental or delta snapshots (store only what changed) combined with periodic full snapshots for compaction, rather than full copies on every save. Delta snapshots reduce memory at the cost of restore complexity; periodic full snapshots serve as reliable compaction points.

In languages with value types (structs, records), prefer those for mementos — they are copied by value naturally, eliminating aliasing bugs without explicit deep-copy logic. Modern C# records, Python frozen dataclasses, and Kotlin data classes are natural memento carriers.

Use the narrow/wide interface split deliberately: expose metadata (name, timestamp, checksum, version label) through the caretaker-facing interface, but keep the full state access behind the originator-facing interface. This prevents accidental state exposure while enabling useful history browsing.

For networked or distributed systems, include a version or checksum in the memento so the originator can detect drift, corruption, or mismatched schema before attempting a restore that would leave the system in an inconsistent state.

When the originator holds open resources (file handles, sockets, DB connections), exclude them from the snapshot and re-establish them on restore — a memento that captures a closed-file handle or a broken socket cannot restore useful state.

Validate memento integrity before restore: check that the stored state is of the expected type, version, and shape. A memento from an older class version or a different originator instance applied to the wrong object silently corrupts history.

In multi-editor or collaborative scenarios, snapshot the edit clone, not the live shared document: edit on a private clone, create the memento from the clone on commit, or discard the clone on cancel. Editing the live shared object risks exposing unconfirmed changes to other clients or background tasks.

Consider thread-safety when the originator is accessed concurrently: snapshotting and restoring from multiple threads without synchronization produces nondeterministic history. Serialize access through the originator or use copy-on-write concurrency models.

related_patterns_notes.command: Command and Memento are frequently composed: a Command holds the memento it needs to reverse itself, turning a sequence of changes into a single undoable unit. Command provides the 'what to undo' semantics; Memento provides the 'how to undo' snapshot.
related_patterns_notes.state: State and Memento both represent state snapshots, but State delegates state switching to the object itself (self-transition), whereas Memento captures the full internal state for later external restore. Use State for objects that know their own transitions; use Memento when an external caretaker must drive restore without knowing the state's shape.
related_patterns_notes.prototype: Prototype creates a copy of an object for immediate use; Memento creates a copy for deferred restore. A shallow-prototype clone has the same aliasing risk as a shallow memento — both require deep copying to freeze shared mutable state.
related_patterns_notes.iterator: Iterator can enumerate a sequence of mementos to provide history traversal (e.g., a slider over undo states), with each memento serving as a snapshot waypoint in a linear history.
related_patterns_notes.immutable-object: Immutable objects naturally sidestep the aliasing problem in mementos — if the originator's state is immutable, a reference copy IS a snapshot, and no deep copy is needed. Memento and immutable-object are complementary: immutability simplifies snapshot correctness, and memento provides a controlled restore path.
related_patterns_notes.copy-on-write: Copy-on-write defers the copy until a mutation occurs; Memento copies immediately on save. Both avoid exposing live mutable state, but COW optimizes for read-heavy workloads while Memento optimizes for restore correctness at the cost of immediate copy overhead.
related_patterns_notes.event-sourcing: Event Sourcing stores the full append-only history of domain events as the source of truth and replays events to reconstruct state; Memento stores explicit state snapshots as a fallback or optimization. Event sourcing is a complete architecture; Memento is a local pattern. Memento snapshots can serve as checkpoints in an event-sourced system to avoid replaying the full event log from genesis.
